newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: FEATURE - GUATEMALA'S STRANGE FRUIT: lynching victims.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - GUATEMALA'S STRANGE FRUIT: lynching victims.

text.p: Filiberto Garcia says he wants a proper trial for the men who killed his son -- not the kind of justice the mob meted out when it beat, shot and burned his boy alive for alleged involvement in a murder.

Gilberto Garcia, 16, a student, and two rancher friends left their homes near Guatemala's capital on Aug. 10 to drive three hours to Joyabaj, a remote mountain town in central Guatemala. On their trip to buy cattle the three young men stopped at a canteen where one of them got in a brawl and shot and killed a man.
The three fled the scene but police quickly caught them, only to lose them to an enraged mob that dragged them out of jail, doused them with fuel and set them on fire.

The gruesome incineration of Garcia, Gustavo Lutin, 18, and Jose Francisco Berreondo, 21, brought incidents of mob violence in Guatemala this year to more than 100, with a death toll of 15 to 31 according to differing estimates by newspapers and police.

Frustrated with an inept justice system and a legacy of impunity for criminals with money or human rights abusers with connections to the police or the military, Guatemalans are increasingly taking the law into their own hands.

The frustration is so great that according to a recent poll in La Republica newspaper, 70 percent of Guatemalans agree with citizens who lynched criminals even while 47 percent recognise suspects should be turned over to police.

Lynchings have captured the news throughout the year. In one of the most horrifying incidents, on March 22 in the southern Guatemala town of Nueva Concepcion, a mob dragged two alleged kidnappers out of custody and killed and burned them.
In August, there were several lynchings every week. On August 19 villagers in the northern rural town of Tecpan allegedly killed two teenage boys, aged 14 and 17, for stealing chickens.
Minister of the Interior Rodolfo Mendoza said many of the lynched people are minor thieves caught red-handed.

"Our people are not really so violent and bloodthirsty. This ... is the result of years of frustration because there's not a rapid application of justice," said Carlos Escobar, an analyst at the Research and Social Studies Association.

The Association promotes education, workshops and new norms to combat the lynching problem. Prosecutors and police must be trained in investigation and the courts must get sufficient proof in order to dictate appropriate sentences, said Escobar.

A history of death threats to judges, intimidation of prosecutors, pre-trial releases for accused murders that turn into eternal release for the wealthy, and rogue police officers who sabotage investigations all plague Guatemala's justice system.
"The real solution is that the cycle of justice function effectively," Interior Minister Mendoza told Reuters.
In most lynchings, the members of the mob are never identified or brought to justice, so the cycle of frustrated justice continues.
But Filiberto Garcia, a 49-year-old messenger for a government agency who has four surviving children, and the parents of the other young men lynched in Joyabaj are pressuring the system.
Garcia is pleased a judge has ordered the arrest of seven men named in the lynching.

The police said a mob of 500 forced them to give up the three young men, but Garcia said eyewitnesses told him only 15 men participated in the lynchings. They also said his son got on his knees and begged for his life.

Garcia's family can hardly bear the loss of Gilberto, who followed the families pentecostal religion and liked to tame horses. But Filiberto Garcia recognises that the lynched men should have faced trial for the murder one of them commited.
"The law must be fulfilled, because we are the same as them if we commit the same kind of act. Then they would have to force the law to be fulfilled," said Garcia.
Guatemala's culture of violence stemming from a 36-year civil war stands between Garcia and the justice he seeks.
"Guatemala has a sad history of people taking justice into their own hands," said Mendoza, referring to past killings by security forces intent on routing out leftist rebels.
The minister said this year's spate of lynchings may be the first time large mobs have pulled people out of jail and threatened police officers to get their hands on suspected criminals.
